argument: This episode pairs Max Weber's account of rationalization with Henri Bergson's critique of spatialized time. Weber argues that the Enlightenment project of applying scientific efficiency to every social domain - government, economy, the self - delivers real goods (freedom, equality, technology, knowledge) but always at a hidden cost, trapping modern people in an 'iron cage' of bureaucratic impersonality, identity-anxiety, technological alienation, and disenchantment. Bergson then argues that this same rationalizing impulse leads us to falsely understand even non-spatial things like time through spatial metaphors, when reality, especially lived time or 'duration,' is better understood as continuous, unfolding process rather than static, measurable instants.
keyIdeas: 'Rationalization' is the Enlightenment project of applying scientific efficiency to every social domain, breaking society into component parts each optimized on its own terms, in contrast to premodern societies that prioritized endurance and tradition over pure efficiency.

Weber's 'world mastery' names the overarching goal of total human control over nature and society; his characteristic 'yes, but' structure grants that it delivers real goods while insisting every gain carries a hidden cost.

Greater equality within institutions produces bureaucratic impersonality (illustrated by the DMV), because treating people as interchangeable units is what equal treatment actually requires, and modern freedom brings constant identity-anxiety in place of the premodern peasant's stable, unquestioned identity.

Technological alienation describes how technology's self-accelerating nature obsoletes not just old tools but the pieces of life and meaning built around them, so that nothing accumulates sentimental value before it's replaced.

Weber's 'iron cage' describes how modern rationalized existence traps individuals even while delivering real progress, culminating in 'disenchantment' - the world losing its aura of mystery the more thoroughly science explains and controls it; Bergson's sand-dune and movie-theater analogies argue reality, including time, is fundamentally a process ('duration') rather than a static thing that holds still to be measured.
